newsitem.title: UK: Mediterranean and W African crudes remain strong.
newsitem.headline: Mediterranean and W African crudes remain strong.

text.p: Urals crude in the Mediterranean held firm on Wednesday as the timing of the next Iraqi barrels on the market still remained unclear, traders in the region said.
Prompt barrels commanded hefty prices as alternatives were scarce.
One large prompt cargo was heard offered at Dated Brent -60 cents but buyers' ideas for later barrels were some 15-20 cents cheaper.

"But no-one knows where the cut-off point is going to be. Sellers further out don't want to sell too cheaply and buyers want to wait as long as they can in case there will be some Kirkuk barrels," a trader with a major said.
West African barrels continued to move at steady premiums in a relaxed, balanced market.

A third decade August Bonny Medium/Light cargo was heard traded this week at steady to the last done deal at Dated Brent +50 cents for the Light and Dated Brent +20 cents for the Medium, traders said.

Forcados was assessed steady at Dated +32 cents after a deal at this level in the last few days. A partial third decade August cargo was being offered at Dated +30 cents. This was the last unsold August loading Forcados.
A VLCC of Qua Iboe loading August 17-19 was being worked into the U.S. Gulf. One Aug 20-31 cargo remained unsold and market value was seen at Dated +45 cents.

On Tuesday Iraqi envoy to the United Nations, Nizar Hamdoon said he saw no blocks to getting oil sales restarted, but noted that Baghdad must still submit some technical "annexes" to the aid plan currently being reviewed by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan.
The annexes were to be delivered to New York by the weekend, Hamdoon said.

Annan's spokesman said the Secretariat would complete the aid plan review by the end of July. Even then, the oil sales cannot start until Baghdad submits a new pricing mechanism to oil overseers for setting terms of contracts.
Iraq, according to Western diplomats last week, must sell $1 billion of the $2 billion oil accord ceiling in the first 90-day half of the 180-day period.
Since the June 8 resumption of the oil for aid deal, Baghdad has not exported, leaving a small window to move $1 billion in sales ahead of the first period's expiry on September 5.

Unless the United Nations acts to move the start date forward or allow the $2 billion limit to cover the full 180 day period, oil markets could be swamped with Iraqi exports in excess of 1.5 million barrels per day.

"Even at 1.5 million barrels per day they won't make their money ($1 billion). It's a high risk market to get into when you have no idea how much crude they will put on the market. At the moment it looks like they will hit this market with as much as they can manage to get on ships," another sour crude trader said.
